sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title, Tuttle 1990 'Tolowa Prosody - An Interim Report' (ANLA CA990T1990), was located as an open scan at uafanlc.alaska.edu (SSL chain broken; downloaded by automated download -k), scanned (no text, 300 dpi, one tesseract at a time) and read on the page scan; saved with under It is a first-hand, stress-focused analysis from new field data (Seaburg 1976-82 tapes; Tuttle's own work with Berneice Humphrey): Tolowa is 'not classed as a tone language'; stress is assigned by rule - domain bounded by the stem's right edge, stress the last vowel of the domain, stress all full vowels, rightmost stress strongest - and realized as high pitch (adjacent accents: falling + high; utterance-final stem high pitch optionally deleted). This CONTRADICTS the catalog's 'tonal' out-code, which rests only on Bright 1964's 'pitch accent or tone' with no placement rule; the resulting system is morphological/lexical stress (stem + full-vowel conditioned, not syllable-counting), so under the catalog's registers the honest coding is 'disputed: tonal (Bright 1964) vs morphological stress (Tuttle 1990)'. Tuttle herself hedges: 'both stress-like phenomena.. and tone-like phenomena', interim status. The same scan carries her AAA 1990 abstract 'Stress, Accent, and Vowel Length in Tolowa' (p. 229), which reads Bright 1964 as PENULTIMATE stress marked by high pitch with exceptions - a claim absent from the on-disk Bright scanned and at odds with StressTyp2/Gordon's banked 'final'; Bright 1964:104-105 should be re-read for it. The fuller statement, Tuttle's UW M.A. thesis 'Stress and Vowel Length in Tolowa' (1990), remains unlocated online and stays the high-priority acquisition. no shadow libraries used.

new_statements.quote: A. Proposed Rules for Accentuation: 1. The domain of stress is bounded by the right edge of the stem. 2. Stress the last vowel in the domain. 3. Stress all full vowels. 4. The strongest stress in a word is the rightmost stress. B. Phonetic Realization. An accented vowel is realized with high pitch. Generally, if there are two accented vowels in adjacent syllables, the first will be realized as a falling pitch rather than a high pitch. While in single words the rightmost stress is the strongest, an intonational contour exists over utterances which goes from high to low and ends with a boundary low pitch.

new_statements.reading: Tuttle analyses Tolowa prominence as STRESS realized by high pitch, not as tone (p. 1: 'Tolowa is not classed as a tone language'). Placement is morphological and vowel-quality-driven, not syllable-counting: the stem (rightmost morpheme before suffixes) always carries stress; every full (non-schwa) vowel in prefixes or stems is also stressed; suffixes and prefix schwas are unstressed; the rightmost (stem) stress is primary. Adjacent accents surface as falling+high; utterance-final stem high pitch may optionally delete after a stressed vowel (p. 6). She concedes residual 'tone-like' facts (opaque 2pl prefix, three pitch treatments of prefix [e]) and calls the analysis interim. Against the catalog: the 'tonal' out-code rests on Bright's 'pitch accent or tone' with no placement rule; Tuttle supplies a placement rule under a stress analysis (a lexical/morphological stress system, weight-blind but quality-sensitive), so the classification should at least be flagged as disputed between a tonal (Bright) and a morphological-stress (Tuttle) reading. Her AAA abstract further attributes a penultimate-stress rule to Bright 1964, which the on-disk Bright text does not show and which conflicts with StressTyp2's banked 'final'; Bright p. 104-105 needs a fresh page read.

readall_conflicts: No new source was readable, so the standing disagreement in the record is unchanged: the catalog (StressTyp2 via Bright) codes Tolowa as tonal with a final-syllable pattern string, while Tuttle 1990 (already in existing_statements) analyses Tolowa as a stress language (stress realized by high pitch, domain bounded by the right edge of the stem, all full vowels stressed, rightmost stress strongest) and explicitly says Tolowa is not classed as a tone language. Golla 2011, the only work listed for this item, could not settle: the copy consulted is front matter only.

sources.quote: "Bright (1964) describes Tolowa, a Pacific Coast Athapaskan language, as having penultimate stress, marked with high pitch, and a near complementary distribution of long and short full vowels in open and closed syllables. Bright lists exceptions to both rules. In data gathered by Bill Seaburg there are final high pitches and short full vowels. I will argue that the two systems interact: stress appears as high pitch, triggering vowel lengthening; competing accentual high pitch deletes pitch stress, leaving a low-pitched long vowel."
sources.locator: Abstracts of the 89th Annual Meeting, p. 229, entry TUTTLE
sources.note: Reads Bright 1964 as describing PENULTIMATE stress marked by high pitch (with exceptions) - a placement statement that neither the SPA-banked accent quotations nor the interleaved Bright scanned held by the project (sources_slice3/) show, and which contradicts StressTyp2/Gordon's banked 'final' for the same source; Bright 1964:104-105 should be re-read for a penult statement. Tuttle's own claim: stress = high pitch, triggers lengthening; a competing 'accentual' high pitch can delete the stress pitch, leaving a low long vowel (i.e. a lexical pitch accent layer interacting with stress).
